Label the 13 black cells as

\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
A&B&C\\
D&E&\\
F&G&H\\
I&J&\\
K&L&M
\end{array}
\]

where the corners are \(A,C,K,M\).

Each corner has only one adjacent black cell:
\[
A\sim D,\quad C\sim E,\quad K\sim I,\quad M\sim J.
\]
Also, a corner can jump only to \(G\), over that adjacent cell.

If a corner is not the first or last cell of the trail, it must be entered from its adjacent cell and then leave by jumping over that cell to \(G\). Since \(G\) can be visited only once, at most one corner can be an internal cell of the trail. The trail has only two endpoints, so at most \(2+1=3\) corner cells can be visited. Thus at most \(9+3=12\) black cells can be visited.

This bound is attainable. One valid trail is

\[
C \to E \to B \to H \to J \to L \to I \to F \to D \to A \to G \to M.
\]

In coordinates:

\[
(1,5)\to(2,4)\to(1,3)\to(3,5)\to(4,4)\to(5,3)\to(4,2)\to(3,1)\to(2,2)\to(1,1)\to(3,3)\to(5,5).
\]

Here \(B\to H\) jumps over \(E\), \(A\to G\) jumps over \(D\), and \(G\to M\) jumps over \(J\); all other moves are ordinary diagonal moves.

Therefore the maximum number of cells is

\[
\boxed{12}.
\]
